# Chapter 3 — The Hill Will Teach

On Day 3, the morning was already warm when Leo found his grandfather in the garden, moving slowly between the olive trees with his walking stick, stopping sometimes to look at a stone that had worked its way to the surface. Bruno followed two paces behind, the way he always did, his tongue out from the heat.

Leo waited until Marcos had finished turning over a particular stone and was making his way toward the bench under the wide shadow of the largest tree. He had been turning the question over in his own mind since breakfast—how to ask it, whether to ask it at all—but he had decided on the walk down the garden that the answer would only come if he asked plainly. Marcos respected that. He did not talk down to questions.

"Abuelo," he said, and Marcos turned with the careful attention he gave to everything. "What is really on the other side of the hill? And why doesn't anyone talk about it?"

It was the sort of question that hung in the air for a long moment. Bruno settled himself in the dust beside the bench, circled three times exactly, and lay down with his nose pointing toward the house. Leo stood with his hands at his sides, waiting.

Marcos did not sit down. He held his walking stick still for a moment, then tapped it twice against the ground—a deliberate, clear sound, like the turning of a page. When he looked up, his eyes held that particular warmth that meant he was about to answer truly, even if the answer came in his own circling way.

"You know," Marcos said slowly, "that the shepherds walk up into the pines in the early morning and come back down at dusk, the way they have for more summers than I have been alive. Do you know why they walk up?"

Leo knew this already. He did not know he knew it, but he did. "The sheep go where the grass is better."

"Yes. They go to eat." Marcos paused, tapping his stick gently once in the dust. "And at night they come back down because the darkness makes it hard to see, and because in the darkness it is harder to follow a path you know by day. They know the other side of the hill the way you know the rooms in your house in the dark—they could move through them asleep and find their way. Do you understand?"

Leo nodded, though he was not certain he understood yet.

"The hill is not a wall," Marcos went on, and he turned now to look at the green rise of it, the curve of it against the sky. "It is a border. On this side, there is the village and the house and everyone you know. On the other side, there is everyone who lives there, a house, and lives that go on the way lives do. The hill is not the difference. It is only the ground between one kind of day and another." He turned back to Leo. "Do you know what the hill will teach you?"

"No," Leo said.

"Neither do I. Not because I do not know what is there, but because the hill teaches differently to each person who climbs it. It will show you what you need to see, not what I can tell you." Marcos shifted his weight on the stick. "Why do you suppose people do not talk about it?"

Leo opened his mouth, then closed it. He thought of Rosa's father saying "less interesting than you think," and of the way the shopkeepers changed their voices when anyone mentioned the other side. He thought of his mother saying "before dark" like a spell, like a protection, not like an order. "Because," he said slowly, "maybe they think people should find it themselves?"

Marcos smiled—a real smile that reached his eyes—and tapped his stick once more, gently, against the earth. "The hill will teach," he said again. "That is all I know, and that is all you need."

He sat down then, slowly, the way old men do, settling himself into the bench as if he were fitting back into the shape of it. He was done speaking. Leo could feel that the way you feel the end of a story—not because someone says the story is over, but because you know, without being told, that there is nothing left to say.

He stood in the dust of the garden, understanding that this was all Marcos would offer him, and that the offering itself was a kind of trust. The old man had not told him what to do or what to expect, had given him no directions or promises or warnings. He had simply said that the hill would teach, and that Leo was old enough to be taught by it.

Bruno lifted his head, looking at the boy from where he lay, his small terrier eyes alert and waiting.

Leo looked down at his own hands—empty now, the way they had been yesterday at the fountain when Rosa asked him where he was going. Empty the way they would need to be if he was going to climb, to hold his balance, to find his own way down the other side.

The day stretched ahead of him, and the hill was waiting, and he understood now that he had the only answer Marcos could give him: that he would have to go and see, and trust that the going and the seeing would be enough. His grandfather's silence was not an absence of knowledge. It was a kind of faith.

=== STORY BIBLE — bible/world.md (in full) ===
# The World of The Other Side of the Hill

[NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] lives in a house at the edge of a small village in a landscape of stone and scrub, where the Mediterranean heat eases in the evening and the cicadas know when to start their song. The house is old enough to have stories but young enough to still live in them. Behind it rises a hill that [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] has never crossed, though he has stood at its foot a hundred times and wondered what a person might find there. This summer, the summer he turns ten, he is old enough—or brave enough, or curious enough—to go and see. His scruffy terrier Bruno will come with him. His fossil, his stones, his grandfather's wooden treehouse observatory, and the dark that waits when the sun goes down: all of these are part of the story of that crossing.

## Places

- **The House and Garden** — A stone house with a wide kitchen where the family gathers. The garden is dry and full of olive trees, wild rosemary, and the long shadow the house casts on summer afternoons. The wooden treehouse observatory stands built into the broad old fig tree near the back wall, reached by a short wooden ladder nailed to the trunk: it was built two summers ago from planks and a scavenged window, with a cardboard tube for a telescope and a lens of polished glass. It creaks when the wind moves the branches and smells of dust and pencil marks where [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] has labeled the stars on the inside boards. No one has taken it down.

- **The Stone Collection** — Kept in a jar by [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO]'s bedroom window: smooth stones from beaches and riverbeds, each chosen for its shape or color or the way light moves through it. There are forty-three of them. He knows each one's story.

- **Captain Crunch** — The fossil found on the beach at Cadaques two summers ago, the size of a child's hand, shaped like a sleeping animal or a ship's anchor depending on the light. It sits on the shelf above [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO]'s desk, next to a drawing he made of what creature it might have been.

- **The Hill** — Rising behind the house, steep enough to demand respect, covered in low pine, wild thyme, and stones that roll underfoot. The path up it is used by shepherds but no one speaks about what is on the other side. The hill is old in a way the house is not.

- **The Village** — Houses clustered around a small plaza with a fountain, a baker, a bar where men drink coffee and argue, a schoolroom. It is small enough that [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] knows all the shopkeepers by their faces and most by name. The baker's daughter is his age. People move slowly in the heat.

## People and Groups

- **[NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO]'s Family** — His parents, who want him safe and home by dusk but who understand a boy must learn the shape of the world. They worry about the dark and about the hill in equal measure. They are wrong about how brave he is, but right about how much the dark frightens him.

- **The Grandfather** — A man who built a wooden treehouse observatory and did not laugh when [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] named a fossil after a cereal. He knows more about the hill than he tells. He wants [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] to find his own answers. He walks slowly and tells stories that circle around the truth rather than naming it.

- **The Village** — Shopkeepers, shepherds, the baker and her family: people who have lived here for generations and who have opinions about the hill that range from disinterest to respect. They think the hill is private in a way that has nothing to do with ownership. They are right about that.

- **Whoever Is on the Other Side** — Not yet known. Not yet met. The reason for the journey.

## Rules

- **R1.** [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] must stop travelling when the sun touches the horizon, wherever he is—at home or on either side of the hill. Waiting for daylight where he has stopped is obedience to this rule, not a breach of it.

- **R2.** When Bruno whines and presses his body against [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO]'s leg, that is a warning he must notice, weigh, and speak aloud about, but may choose to go forward past. When Bruno stops dead and turns back, that is a refusal and [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] goes no further that way.

- **R3.** The wooden treehouse observatory belongs to both [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] and his grandfather; neither may promise it or lend it without the other saying yes.

- **R4.** When the sun is fully down, distance becomes unreliable—a path [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] knows in daylight becomes unfindable, and walking further only carries him further from where he meant to be rather than nearer. Fear in the dark is not a small thing.

- **R5.** Supper is at the same hour every night, and the family sits to it then. Whoever is not yet home has a place laid and a plate kept warm until he arrives.

- **R6.** When asked a direct question out of curiosity, the grandfather answers truthfully but in a story that circles the answer. When the same question is asked by someone who has already been to the place and can carry the answer, he answers plainly and in one sentence.

- **R7.** The hill does not shout—voices carry differently there, and distances are harder to judge; a person calling from the other side sounds both nearer and farther than she truly is.

## The feel of it

This book lives in the hours when a ten-year-old is most himself: curious, honest, stubborn, afraid of the dark but pretending not to be. The warmth is in the details—the shape of a stone, the way a dog sleeps, an old man who remembers things. The funny is small and true: a treehouse observatory built by hand, a fossil named after breakfast cereal, the way a child's logic works when an adult is listening. The fear is real and not dismissed—the dark is genuinely frightening, and bravery means going forward anyway—but it is held by the warmth of the dog at his side and the grandfather's voice in memory. This is a book about being on the edge of something larger than yourself, and choosing to step forward.

Bruno
Marcos

### [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO]
- **[NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO]** — the protagonist, ten years old; curious, observant, brave though he denies his fear

Wants: to discover what lies on the other side of the hill and to be certain he is brave enough to go alone.

Wrong about: how invisible his fear is to the people who love him; they see him clearly.

Speaks: Direct and honest, with a habit of asking questions rather than making statements. When frightened, he hesitates and changes the subject. His voice is steady until it isn't.

Habit: Turns smooth stones over in his palms when thinking or anxious, reading their shape by touch as much as by sight.

### Bruno
- **Bruno** — scruffy terrier, [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO]'s constant companion; loyal, sensible, afraid of deep shadow but braver than he pretends

Wants: to follow [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] and keep him safe, and to sleep warm at the foot of his bed.

Wrong about: Nothing much. His instincts about danger are correct.

Speaks: Through body language—whines sharply when frightened, circles before settling, stands close when anxious. His bark is quick and sharp when happy or alert.

Habit: Sleeps at the foot of [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO]'s bed every night, and circles three times before lying down anywhere.

### Marcos
- **Marcos** — the grandfather; patient, knowing, a builder of the wooden treehouse observatory; he walks slowly and speaks in stories

Wants: For [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] to find his own answers rather than be given them; to see the boy become himself.

Wrong about: That silence and stories alone are enough; sometimes a ten-year-old needs a direct answer.

Speaks: In circles and stories, often answering a question with another question. His voice is quiet and requires listening closely. He pauses for a long time before speaking, as if weighing words.

Habit: Pauses before answering, and taps his walking stick twice against the ground when about to tell the truth.

### Rosa
- **Rosa** — the baker's daughter, same age as [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO]; practical, quick-thinking, braver than he is about admitting what frightens her

Wants: An adventure beyond the bakery and the village square; a friend who understands wanting to know what's beyond.

Wrong about: That [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] wants to do this alone; she does not ask, but she is meant to help.

Speaks: Quickly and directly, with humor and jokes when uncertain. Her words tumble out, and she laughs at her own nervous rambling. Flour dust marks her wherever she goes.

Habit: Brushes flour from her sleeves and apron without noticing she is doing it, a leftover from mornings in her mother's kitchen.

### Elena
- **Elena** — a girl, twelve years old, living with her grandmother on the other side of the hill; quiet, observant, rooted to the land

Wants: To understand who climbs the hill and why; to know if anyone else collects the small treasures the earth gives up.

Wrong about: That the other side of the hill is as mysterious to others as her own life is to the village below.

Speaks: Carefully and slowly, as if testing each word. She asks simple questions that reach deeper than expected. Her voice is smaller than a ten-year-old's but steady.

Habit: Picks up small objects—pebbles, seeds, shells, anything the hill or the wind has left—and examines them closely, turning them over in her hands as if reading their stories.

# The World of The Other Side of the Hill

[NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] lives in a house at the edge of a small village in a landscape of stone and scrub, where the Mediterranean heat eases in the evening and the cicadas know when to start their song. The house is old enough to have stories but young enough to still live in them. Behind it rises a hill that [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] has never crossed, though he has stood at its foot a hundred times and wondered what a person might find there. This summer, the summer he turns ten, he is old enough—or brave enough, or curious enough—to go and see. His scruffy terrier Bruno will come with him. His fossil, his stones, his grandfather's wooden treehouse observatory, and the dark that waits when the sun goes down: all of these are part of the story of that crossing.

## Places

- **The House and Garden** — A stone house with a wide kitchen where the family gathers. The garden is dry and full of olive trees, wild rosemary, and the long shadow the house casts on summer afternoons. The wooden treehouse observatory stands built into the broad old fig tree near the back wall, reached by a short wooden ladder nailed to the trunk: it was built two summers ago from planks and a scavenged window, with a cardboard tube for a telescope and a lens of polished glass. It creaks when the wind moves the branches and smells of dust and pencil marks where [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] has labeled the stars on the inside boards. No one has taken it down.

- **The Stone Collection** — Kept in a jar by [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO]'s bedroom window: smooth stones from beaches and riverbeds, each chosen for its shape or color or the way light moves through it. There are forty-three of them. He knows each one's story.

- **Captain Crunch** — The fossil found on the beach at Cadaques two summers ago, the size of a child's hand, shaped like a sleeping animal or a ship's anchor depending on the light. It sits on the shelf above [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO]'s desk, next to a drawing he made of what creature it might have been.

- **The Hill** — Rising behind the house, steep enough to demand respect, covered in low pine, wild thyme, and stones that roll underfoot. The path up it is used by shepherds but no one speaks about what is on the other side. The hill is old in a way the house is not.

- **The Village** — Houses clustered around a small plaza with a fountain, a baker, a bar where men drink coffee and argue, a schoolroom. It is small enough that [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] knows all the shopkeepers by their faces and most by name. The baker's daughter is his age. People move slowly in the heat.

## People and Groups

- **[NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO]'s Family** — His parents, who want him safe and home by dusk but who understand a boy must learn the shape of the world. They worry about the dark and about the hill in equal measure. They are wrong about how brave he is, but right about how much the dark frightens him.

- **The Grandfather** — A man who built a wooden treehouse observatory and did not laugh when [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] named a fossil after a cereal. He knows more about the hill than he tells. He wants [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] to find his own answers. He walks slowly and tells stories that circle around the truth rather than naming it.

- **The Village** — Shopkeepers, shepherds, the baker and her family: people who have lived here for generations and who have opinions about the hill that range from disinterest to respect. They think the hill is private in a way that has nothing to do with ownership. They are right about that.

- **Whoever Is on the Other Side** — Not yet known. Not yet met. The reason for the journey.

## Rules

- **R1.** [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] must stop travelling when the sun touches the horizon, wherever he is—at home or on either side of the hill. Waiting for daylight where he has stopped is obedience to this rule, not a breach of it.

- **R2.** When Bruno whines and presses his body against [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO]'s leg, that is a warning he must notice, weigh, and speak aloud about, but may choose to go forward past. When Bruno stops dead and turns back, that is a refusal and [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] goes no further that way.

- **R3.** The wooden treehouse observatory belongs to both [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] and his grandfather; neither may promise it or lend it without the other saying yes.

- **R4.** When the sun is fully down, distance becomes unreliable—a path [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] knows in daylight becomes unfindable, and walking further only carries him further from where he meant to be rather than nearer. Fear in the dark is not a small thing.

- **R5.** Supper is at the same hour every night, and the family sits to it then. Whoever is not yet home has a place laid and a plate kept warm until he arrives.

- **R6.** When asked a direct question out of curiosity, the grandfather answers truthfully but in a story that circles the answer. When the same question is asked by someone who has already been to the place and can carry the answer, he answers plainly and in one sentence.

- **R7.** The hill does not shout—voices carry differently there, and distances are harder to judge; a person calling from the other side sounds both nearer and farther than she truly is.

## The feel of it

This book lives in the hours when a ten-year-old is most himself: curious, honest, stubborn, afraid of the dark but pretending not to be. The warmth is in the details—the shape of a stone, the way a dog sleeps, an old man who remembers things. The funny is small and true: a treehouse observatory built by hand, a fossil named after breakfast cereal, the way a child's logic works when an adult is listening. The fear is real and not dismissed—the dark is genuinely frightening, and bravery means going forward anyway—but it is held by the warmth of the dog at his side and the grandfather's voice in memory. This is a book about being on the edge of something larger than yourself, and choosing to step forward.

- **Bruno** — scruffy terrier, [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO]'s constant companion; loyal, sensible, afraid of deep shadow but braver than he pretends

# Chapter 10 — The Other Side Now

The last plate was cleared and his mother had begun to stack them by habit, the rhythm of any ordinary evening, when [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] looked up from the table and asked the question plainly.

"Can I climb the hill again soon? With the same rule—home before dark?"

His father set down his glass and considered this not as a breach but as a reasonable request from a boy who had climbed a hill and lived to ask for another morning. His mother's hand paused on the table. Marcos, still in the corner chair, did not move.

"Yes," his father said. "The same rule holds."

This was exactly the answer [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] had hoped for and somehow did not expect. He felt something settle in his chest—not the hammering anticipation that had driven him up the hill four days ago, but something quieter: the knowledge that the world was larger than he had believed, and that he could move through it again.

Before he could speak further, there was a sound at the gate—a small, polite knock. It was Rosa, flour dust still on her sleeves though the bakery had closed hours ago. She stood in the kitchen doorway with the air of someone who had been waiting and had finally decided on courage.

"[NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO]?" she said, her words tumbling out quickly. "My mother said you would tell me everything about the other side, and I said you would not dare to, and then I said I would come and make you, and I have been at the gate since supper started because I was nervous about interrupting, but now I am here." She stopped for breath. "Can I come next time? When you climb again? I promise I am not afraid of the dark—well, I am, but only a small amount, and I can carry things."

[NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] felt Bruno shift against his leg, tail thumping softly. He looked at Rosa's determined face and understood that she had been waiting not to hear the story, but to be asked into the next one.

"Yes," he said. "Come with us."

His mother smiled in the way that suggested this was exactly what she had meant when she said he would want to tell Rosa everything. Marcos tapped his walking stick once against the floor—not twice, not yet—and his eyes moved between the two children with an expression of quiet approval.

It was only after Rosa had been sent home with a promise to prepare supplies and a piece of his mother's bread that [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] remembered the other thing, the thing he had been turning over in his mind since he woke this morning.

He thought of Elena in her yard on the far side of the hill, bent over the earth looking for what it had left behind. He thought of showing her the wooden treehouse observatory that he and Marcos had built together, the one that smelled of dust and pencil marks and time. He thought of her climbing the wooden ladder nailed into the fig tree and seeing the lens polished by his own hands, the cardboard telescope, the boards he had labeled with stars—and then he remembered the truth of it, the rule that lived inside it.

He looked at Marcos.

"Can I show Elena the observatory?" he asked aloud, the way a question should be asked.

The kitchen was still. His mother's hands were quiet on a bowl. His father was watching. Bruno's ears pricked forward, attentive to the tone of something important being said.

Marcos set down his walking stick and tapped it twice against the stone floor.

Tap. Tap.

The sound of truth about to be spoken.

"Yes," Marcos said, his voice steady and thin as old paper. "It is half hers now, too."

[NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] understood this was not quite what the rule said, but it was what the rule meant. The observatory belonged to him and to Marcos in equal measure, and now Marcos was saying yes, plainly, in one sentence, because this was an answer that could be carried. It meant that when [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] climbed the hill again with Rosa, when they reached the far side and found Elena, he could bring her back across and up the wooden ladder into the space that smelled of stars and dust and the work of their own hands.

The evening was cooling toward its end. The light had taken on the quality it always did near sunset—neither truly gold nor truly orange, but something between that made ordinary things look like they were being remembered rather than seen. [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] and Marcos walked together through the house, through the garden where the olive trees cast their long shadows, to the fig tree with its wooden ladder and the treehouse observatory perched in the branches like a bird's careful nest.

Bruno preceded them, his tail high, no tension in his body now—only the simple certainty of a dog who knew his person was safe and his place was beside him.

Marcos climbed first, his movements slow and deliberate, his walking stick left below. [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] followed, feeling the wooden rungs solid beneath his feet, a ladder built by his grandfather's hands and his own patience. The treehouse creaked the way it always did, and that sound was home now, was proof of making something that lasted.

Inside, the space was smaller than the sky it held. The window Marcos had scavenged fitted perfectly, and through it the emerging stars were beginning to appear like small, patient lights. The cardboard telescope stood in its place. The boards around the walls were still marked with [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO]'s pencil labeling: Polaris, Altair, the shape of Cassiopeia he had traced and retraced until he could see it without looking.

Together, without speaking, they climbed to the high shelf where light fell clearest and longest. Marcos held steady while [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] placed Captain Crunch in the exact center—the fossil shaped like a sleeping animal or a ship's anchor, depending on the light. Around it, in a careful circle, he arranged the smooth stones from the jar, each one chosen for its shape or color or the way light moved through it. Forty-three treasures that the earth had given up and that he and Elena both understood how to see.

The light was extraordinary there—the last of the day catching the pale shell of the fossil and the smooth curves of the stones, turning them gold and then copper and then something that had no name. Looking at them, [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] could almost see the rooms where they had been found: the beach at Cadaques, the riverbed that rushed only in spring, the rocky shore of a place he had only heard described.

Below them, through the open door of the observatory, Bruno had circled three times and settled into the dust, his body warm and his eyes closed. The evening was settling toward its quiet. The first true stars were appearing, not the fading ghosts of them but the real lights that would remain through the whole night long.

Marcos stood beside [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO], not speaking, his hand resting on one of the wooden supports that held the treehouse steady. His walking stick remained on the ground far below, and for the moment he was simply present: an old man and a young boy, looking together at the things they had gathered, and at the sky opening above them like a door into a country they had only begun to know.

"Next time," [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] said quietly, "we will show her this."

Marcos nodded. He did not need to say yes twice. The treehouse held their answer in the light on the stones, in the dust where Bruno slept, in the stars that were coming out one by one, faithful and patient, the way they always did.

The other side of the hill was not a mystery anymore. But the world beyond it still had room for wonders.

=== STORY BIBLE — bible/world.md (in full) ===
# The World of The Other Side of the Hill

[NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] lives in a house at the edge of a small village in a landscape of stone and scrub, where the Mediterranean heat eases in the evening and the cicadas know when to start their song. The house is old enough to have stories but young enough to still live in them. Behind it rises a hill that [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] has never crossed, though he has stood at its foot a hundred times and wondered what a person might find there. This summer, the summer he turns ten, he is old enough—or brave enough, or curious enough—to go and see. His scruffy terrier Bruno will come with him. His fossil, his stones, his grandfather's wooden treehouse observatory, and the dark that waits when the sun goes down: all of these are part of the story of that crossing.

## Places

- **The House and Garden** — A stone house with a wide kitchen where the family gathers. The garden is dry and full of olive trees, wild rosemary, and the long shadow the house casts on summer afternoons. The wooden treehouse observatory stands built into the broad old fig tree near the back wall, reached by a short wooden ladder nailed to the trunk: it was built two summers ago from planks and a scavenged window, with a cardboard tube for a telescope and a lens of polished glass. It creaks when the wind moves the branches and smells of dust and pencil marks where [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] has labeled the stars on the inside boards. No one has taken it down.

- **The Stone Collection** — Kept in a jar by [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO]'s bedroom window: smooth stones from beaches and riverbeds, each chosen for its shape or color or the way light moves through it. There are forty-three of them. He knows each one's story.

- **Captain Crunch** — The fossil found on the beach at Cadaques two summers ago, the size of a child's hand, shaped like a sleeping animal or a ship's anchor depending on the light. It sits on the shelf above [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO]'s desk, next to a drawing he made of what creature it might have been.

- **The Hill** — Rising behind the house, steep enough to demand respect, covered in low pine, wild thyme, and stones that roll underfoot. The path up it is used by shepherds but no one speaks about what is on the other side. The hill is old in a way the house is not.

- **The Village** — Houses clustered around a small plaza with a fountain, a baker, a bar where men drink coffee and argue, a schoolroom. It is small enough that [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] knows all the shopkeepers by their faces and most by name. The baker's daughter is his age. People move slowly in the heat.

## People and Groups

- **[NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO]'s Family** — His parents, who want him safe and home by dusk but who understand a boy must learn the shape of the world. They worry about the dark and about the hill in equal measure. They are wrong about how brave he is, but right about how much the dark frightens him.

- **The Grandfather** — A man who built a wooden treehouse observatory and did not laugh when [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] named a fossil after a cereal. He knows more about the hill than he tells. He wants [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] to find his own answers. He walks slowly and tells stories that circle around the truth rather than naming it.

- **The Village** — Shopkeepers, shepherds, the baker and her family: people who have lived here for generations and who have opinions about the hill that range from disinterest to respect. They think the hill is private in a way that has nothing to do with ownership. They are right about that.

- **Whoever Is on the Other Side** — Not yet known. Not yet met. The reason for the journey.

## Rules

- **R1.** [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] must stop travelling when the sun touches the horizon, wherever he is—at home or on either side of the hill. Waiting for daylight where he has stopped is obedience to this rule, not a breach of it.

- **R2.** When Bruno whines and presses his body against [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO]'s leg, that is a warning he must notice, weigh, and speak aloud about, but may choose to go forward past. When Bruno stops dead and turns back, that is a refusal and [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] goes no further that way.

- **R3.** The wooden treehouse observatory belongs to both [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] and his grandfather; neither may promise it or lend it without the other saying yes.

- **R4.** When the sun is fully down, distance becomes unreliable—a path [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] knows in daylight becomes unfindable, and walking further only carries him further from where he meant to be rather than nearer. Fear in the dark is not a small thing.

- **R5.** Supper is at the same hour every night, and the family sits to it then. Whoever is not yet home has a place laid and a plate kept warm until he arrives.

- **R6.** When asked a direct question out of curiosity, the grandfather answers truthfully but in a story that circles the answer. When the same question is asked by someone who has already been to the place and can carry the answer, he answers plainly and in one sentence.

- **R7.** The hill does not shout—voices carry differently there, and distances are harder to judge; a person calling from the other side sounds both nearer and farther than she truly is.

## The feel of it

This book lives in the hours when a ten-year-old is most himself: curious, honest, stubborn, afraid of the dark but pretending not to be. The warmth is in the details—the shape of a stone, the way a dog sleeps, an old man who remembers things. The funny is small and true: a treehouse observatory built by hand, a fossil named after breakfast cereal, the way a child's logic works when an adult is listening. The fear is real and not dismissed—the dark is genuinely frightening, and bravery means going forward anyway—but it is held by the warmth of the dog at his side and the grandfather's voice in memory. This is a book about being on the edge of something larger than yourself, and choosing to step forward.

# Chapter 10 — The Other Side Now

The last plate was cleared and his mother had begun to stack them by habit, the rhythm of any ordinary evening, when [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] looked up from the table and asked the question plainly.

"Can I climb the hill again soon? With the same rule—home before dark?"

His father set down his glass and considered this not as a breach but as a reasonable request from a boy who had climbed a hill and lived to ask for another morning. His mother's hand paused on the table. Marcos, still in the corner chair, did not move.

"Yes," his father said. "The same rule holds."

This was exactly the answer [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] had hoped for and somehow did not expect. He felt something settle in his chest—not the hammering anticipation that had driven him up the hill four days ago, but something quieter: the knowledge that the world was larger than he had believed, and that he could move through it again.

Before he could speak further, there was a sound at the gate—a small, polite knock. It was Rosa, flour dust still on her sleeves though the bakery had closed hours ago. She stood in the kitchen doorway with the air of someone who had been waiting and had finally decided on courage.

"[NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO]?" she said, her words tumbling out quickly. "My mother said you would tell me everything about the other side, and I said you would not dare to, and then I said I would come and make you, and I have been at the gate since supper started because I was nervous about interrupting, but now I am here." She stopped for breath. "Can I come next time? When you climb again? I promise I am not afraid of the dark—well, I am, but only a small amount, and I can carry things."

[NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] felt Bruno shift against his leg, tail thumping softly. He looked at Rosa's determined face and understood that she had been waiting not to hear the story, but to be asked into the next one.

"Yes," he said. "Come with us."

His mother smiled in the way that suggested this was exactly what she had meant when she said he would want to tell Rosa everything. Marcos tapped his walking stick once against the floor—not twice, not yet—and his eyes moved between the two children with an expression of quiet approval.

It was only after Rosa had been sent home with a promise to prepare supplies and a piece of his mother's bread that [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] remembered the other thing, the thing he had been turning over in his mind since he woke this morning.

He thought of Elena in her yard on the far side of the hill, bent over the earth looking for what it had left behind. He thought of showing her the wooden treehouse observatory that he and Marcos had built together, the one that smelled of dust and pencil marks and time. He thought of her climbing the wooden ladder nailed into the fig tree and seeing the lens polished by his own hands, the cardboard telescope, the boards he had labeled with stars—and then he remembered the truth of it, the rule that lived inside it.

He looked at Marcos.

"Can I show Elena the observatory?" he asked aloud, the way a question should be asked.

The kitchen was still. His mother's hands were quiet on a bowl. His father was watching. Bruno's ears pricked forward, attentive to the tone of something important being said.

Marcos set down his walking stick and tapped it twice against the stone floor.

Tap. Tap.

The sound of truth about to be spoken.

"Yes," Marcos said, his voice steady and thin as old paper. "It is half hers now, too."

[NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] understood this was not quite what the rule said, but it was what the rule meant. The observatory belonged to him and to Marcos in equal measure, and now Marcos was saying yes, plainly, in one sentence, because this was an answer that could be carried. It meant that when [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] climbed the hill again with Rosa, when they reached the far side and found Elena, he could bring her back across and up the wooden ladder into the space that smelled of stars and dust and the work of their own hands.

The evening was cooling toward its end. The light had taken on the quality it always did near sunset—neither truly gold nor truly orange, but something between that made ordinary things look like they were being remembered rather than seen. [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] and Marcos walked together through the house, through the garden where the olive trees cast their long shadows, to the fig tree with its wooden ladder and the treehouse observatory perched in the branches like a bird's careful nest.

Bruno preceded them, his tail high, no tension in his body now—only the simple certainty of a dog who knew his person was safe and his place was beside him.

Marcos climbed first, his movements slow and deliberate, his walking stick left below. [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] followed, feeling the wooden rungs solid beneath his feet, a ladder built by his grandfather's hands and his own patience. The treehouse creaked the way it always did, and that sound was home now, was proof of making something that lasted.

Inside, the space was smaller than the sky it held. The window Marcos had scavenged fitted perfectly, and through it the emerging stars were beginning to appear like small, patient lights. The cardboard telescope stood in its place. The boards around the walls were still marked with [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO]'s pencil labeling: Polaris, Altair, the shape of Cassiopeia he had traced and retraced until he could see it without looking.

Together, without speaking, they climbed to the high shelf where light fell clearest and longest. Marcos held steady while [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] placed Captain Crunch in the exact center—the fossil shaped like a sleeping animal or a ship's anchor, depending on the light. Around it, in a careful circle, he arranged the smooth stones from the jar, each one chosen for its shape or color or the way light moved through it. Forty-three treasures that the earth had given up and that he and Elena both understood how to see.

The light was extraordinary there—the last of the day catching the pale shell of the fossil and the smooth curves of the stones, turning them gold and then copper and then something that had no name. Looking at them, [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] could almost see the rooms where they had been found: the beach at Cadaques, the riverbed that rushed only in spring, the rocky shore of a place he had only heard described.

Below them, through the open door of the observatory, Bruno had circled three times and settled into the dust, his body warm and his eyes closed. The evening was settling toward its quiet. The first true stars were appearing, not the fading ghosts of them but the real lights that would remain through the whole night long.

Marcos stood beside [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO], not speaking, his hand resting on one of the wooden supports that held the treehouse steady. His walking stick remained on the ground far below, and for the moment he was simply present: an old man and a young boy, looking together at the things they had gathered, and at the sky opening above them like a door into a country they had only begun to know.

"Next time," [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] said quietly, "we will show her this."

Marcos nodded. He did not need to say yes twice. The treehouse held their answer in the light on the stones, in the dust where Bruno slept, in the stars that were coming out one by one, faithful and patient, the way they always did.

The other side of the hill was not a mystery anymore. But the world beyond it still had room for wonders.

# The World of The Other Side of the Hill

[NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] lives in a house at the edge of a small village in a landscape of stone and scrub, where the Mediterranean heat eases in the evening and the cicadas know when to start their song. Behind it rises a hill that [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] has never crossed, though he has stood at its foot a hundred times and wondered what a person might find there. This summer, the summer he turns ten, he is old enough—or brave enough, or curious enough—to go and see. His scruffy terrier Bruno will come with him. - **The Stone Collection** — Kept in a jar by [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO]'s bedroom window: smooth stones from beaches and riverbeds, each chosen for its shape or color or the way light moves through it. There are forty-three of them. He knows each one's story.

- **Captain Crunch** — The fossil found on the beach at Cadaques two summers ago, the size of a child's hand, shaped like a sleeping animal or a ship's anchor depending on the light. It sits on the shelf above [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO]'s desk, next to a drawing he made of what creature it might have been.

- **The Hill** — Rising behind the house, steep enough to demand respect, covered in low pine, wild thyme, and stones that roll underfoot. The path up it is used by shepherds but no one speaks about what is on the other side. The hill is old in a way the house is not.

- **The Village** — Houses clustered around a small plaza with a fountain, a baker, a bar where men drink coffee and argue, a schoolroom. It is small enough that [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] knows all the shopkeepers by their faces and most by name. The baker's daughter is his age. People move slowly in the heat.

## People and Groups

- **[NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO]'s Family** — His parents, who want him safe and home by dusk but who understand a boy must learn the shape of the world. They worry about the dark and about the hill in equal measure. They are wrong about how brave he is, but right about how much the dark frightens him.

- **The Grandfather** — A man who built a wooden treehouse observatory and did not laugh when [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] named a fossil after a cereal. He knows more about the hill than he tells. He wants [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] to find his own answers. He walks slowly and tells stories that circle around the truth rather than naming it.

- **The Village** — Shopkeepers, shepherds, the baker and her family: people who have lived here for generations and who have opinions about the hill that range from disinterest to respect. They think the hill is private in a way that has nothing to do with ownership. They are right about that.

- **Whoever Is on the Other Side** — Not yet known. Not yet met. The reason for the journey.

- **R1.** [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] must stop travelling when the sun touches the horizon, wherever he is—at home or on either side of the hill. Waiting for daylight where he has stopped is obedience to this rule, not a breach of it.

- **R2.** When Bruno whines and presses his body against [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO]'s leg, that is a warning he must notice, weigh, and speak aloud about, but may choose to go forward past. When Bruno stops dead and turns back, that is a refusal and [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] goes no further that way.

- **R5.** Supper is at the same hour every night, and the family sits to it then. Whoever is not yet home has a place laid and a plate kept warm until he arrives.

# Chapter 10 — The Other Side Now

The last plate was cleared and his mother had begun to stack them by habit, the rhythm of any ordinary evening, when [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] looked up from the table and asked the question plainly.

"Can I climb the hill again soon? With the same rule—home before dark?"

His father set down his glass and considered this not as a breach but as a reasonable request from a boy who had climbed a hill and lived to ask for another morning. His mother's hand paused on the table. Marcos, still in the corner chair, did not move.

"Yes," his father said. "The same rule holds."

This was exactly the answer [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] had hoped for and somehow did not expect. He felt something settle in his chest—not the hammering anticipation that had driven him up the hill four days ago, but something quieter: the knowledge that the world was larger than he had believed, and that he could move through it again.

Before he could speak further, there was a sound at the gate—a small, polite knock. It was Rosa, flour dust still on her sleeves though the bakery had closed hours ago. She stood in the kitchen doorway with the air of someone who had been waiting and had finally decided on courage.

"[NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO]?" she said, her words tumbling out quickly. "My mother said you would tell me everything about the other side, and I said you would not dare to, and then I said I would come and make you, and I have been at the gate since supper started because I was nervous about interrupting, but now I am here." She stopped for breath. "Can I come next time? When you climb again? I promise I am not afraid of the dark—well, I am, but only a small amount, and I can carry things."

[NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] felt Bruno shift against his leg, tail thumping softly. He looked at Rosa's determined face and understood that she had been waiting not to hear the story, but to be asked into the next one.

"Yes," he said. "Come with us."

His mother smiled in the way that suggested this was exactly what she had meant when she said he would want to tell Rosa everything. Marcos tapped his walking stick once against the floor—not twice, not yet—and his eyes moved between the two children with an expression of quiet approval.

It was only after Rosa had been sent home with a promise to prepare supplies and a piece of his mother's bread that [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] remembered the other thing, the thing he had been turning over in his mind since he woke this morning.

He thought of Elena in her yard on the far side of the hill, bent over the earth looking for what it had left behind. He thought of showing her the wooden treehouse observatory that he and Marcos had built together, the one that smelled of dust and pencil marks and time. He thought of her climbing the wooden ladder nailed into the fig tree and seeing the lens polished by his own hands, the cardboard telescope, the boards he had labeled with stars—and then he remembered the truth of it, the rule that lived inside it.

He looked at Marcos.

"Can I show Elena the observatory?" he asked aloud, the way a question should be asked.

The kitchen was still. His mother's hands were quiet on a bowl. His father was watching. Bruno's ears pricked forward, attentive to the tone of something important being said.

Marcos set down his walking stick and tapped it twice against the stone floor.

Tap. Tap.

The sound of truth about to be spoken.

"Yes," Marcos said, his voice steady and thin as old paper. "It is half hers now, too."

[NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] understood this was not quite what the rule said, but it was what the rule meant. The observatory belonged to him and to Marcos in equal measure, and now Marcos was saying yes, plainly, in one sentence, because this was an answer that could be carried. It meant that when [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] climbed the hill again with Rosa, when they reached the far side and found Elena, he could bring her back across and up the wooden ladder into the space that smelled of stars and dust and the work of their own hands.

The evening was cooling toward its end. The light had taken on the quality it always did near sunset—neither truly gold nor truly orange, but something between that made ordinary things look like they were being remembered rather than seen. [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] and Marcos walked together through the house, through the garden where the olive trees cast their long shadows, to the fig tree with its wooden ladder and the treehouse observatory perched in the branches like a bird's careful nest.

Bruno preceded them, his tail high, no tension in his body now—only the simple certainty of a dog who knew his person was safe and his place was beside him.

Marcos climbed first, his movements slow and deliberate, his walking stick left below. [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] followed, feeling the wooden rungs solid beneath his feet, a ladder built by his grandfather's hands and his own patience. The treehouse creaked the way it always did, and that sound was home now, was proof of making something that lasted.

Inside, the space was smaller than the sky it held. The window Marcos had scavenged fitted perfectly, and through it the emerging stars were beginning to appear like small, patient lights. The cardboard telescope stood in its place. The boards around the walls were still marked with [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO]'s pencil labeling: Polaris, Altair, the shape of Cassiopeia he had traced and retraced until he could see it without looking.

Together, without speaking, they climbed to the high shelf where light fell clearest and longest. Marcos held steady while [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] placed Captain Crunch in the exact center—the fossil shaped like a sleeping animal or a ship's anchor, depending on the light. Around it, in a careful circle, he arranged the smooth stones from the jar, each one chosen for its shape or color or the way light moved through it. Forty-three treasures that the earth had given up and that he and Elena both understood how to see.

The light was extraordinary there—the last of the day catching the pale shell of the fossil and the smooth curves of the stones, turning them gold and then copper and then something that had no name. Looking at them, [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] could almost see the rooms where they had been found: the beach at Cadaques, the riverbed that rushed only in spring, the rocky shore of a place he had only heard described.

Below them, through the open door of the observatory, Bruno had circled three times and settled into the dust, his body warm and his eyes closed. The evening was settling toward its quiet. The first true stars were appearing, not the fading ghosts of them but the real lights that would remain through the whole night long.

Marcos stood beside [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO], not speaking, his hand resting on one of the wooden supports that held the treehouse steady. His walking stick remained on the ground far below, and for the moment he was simply present: an old man and a young boy, looking together at the things they had gathered, and at the sky opening above them like a door into a country they had only begun to know.

"Next time," [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] said quietly, "we will show her this."

Marcos nodded. He did not need to say yes twice. The treehouse held their answer in the light on the stones, in the dust where Bruno slept, in the stars that were coming out one by one, faithful and patient, the way they always did.

The other side of the hill was not a mystery anymore. But the world beyond it still had room for wonders.

- **Day and when**: Day 5, evening

# Chapter 10 — The Other Side Now

The last plate was cleared and his mother had begun to stack them by habit, the rhythm of any ordinary evening, when [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] looked up from the table and asked the question plainly.

"Can I climb the hill again soon? With the same rule—home before dark?"

His father set down his glass and considered this not as a breach but as a reasonable request from a boy who had climbed a hill and lived to ask for another morning. His mother's hand paused on the table. Marcos, still in the corner chair, did not move.

"Yes," his father said. "The same rule holds."

This was exactly the answer [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] had hoped for and somehow did not expect. He felt something settle in his chest—not the hammering anticipation that had driven him up the hill four days ago, but something quieter: the knowledge that the world was larger than he had believed, and that he could move through it again.

Before he could speak further, there was a sound at the gate—a small, polite knock. It was Rosa, flour dust still on her sleeves though the bakery had closed hours ago. She stood in the kitchen doorway with the air of someone who had been waiting and had finally decided on courage.

"[NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO]?" she said, her words tumbling out quickly. "My mother said you would tell me everything about the other side, and I said you would not dare to, and then I said I would come and make you, and I have been at the gate since supper started because I was nervous about interrupting, but now I am here." She stopped for breath. "Can I come next time? When you climb again? I promise I am not afraid of the dark—well, I am, but only a small amount, and I can carry things."

[NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] felt Bruno shift against his leg, tail thumping softly. He looked at Rosa's determined face and understood that she had been waiting not to hear the story, but to be asked into the next one.

"Yes," he said. "Come with us."

His mother smiled in the way that suggested this was exactly what she had meant when she said he would want to tell Rosa everything. Marcos tapped his walking stick once against the floor—not twice, not yet—and his eyes moved between the two children with an expression of quiet approval.

It was only after Rosa had been sent home with a promise to prepare supplies and a piece of his mother's bread that [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] remembered the other thing, the thing he had been turning over in his mind since he woke this morning.

He thought of Elena in her yard on the far side of the hill, bent over the earth looking for what it had left behind. He thought of showing her the wooden treehouse observatory that he and Marcos had built together, the one that smelled of dust and pencil marks and time. He thought of her climbing the wooden ladder nailed into the fig tree and seeing the lens polished by his own hands, the cardboard telescope, the boards he had labeled with stars—and then he remembered the truth of it, the rule that lived inside it.

He looked at Marcos.

"Can I show Elena the observatory?" he asked aloud, the way a question should be asked.

The kitchen was still. His mother's hands were quiet on a bowl. His father was watching. Bruno's ears pricked forward, attentive to the tone of something important being said.

Marcos set down his walking stick and tapped it twice against the stone floor.

Tap. Tap.

The sound of truth about to be spoken.

"Yes," Marcos said, his voice steady and thin as old paper. "It is half hers now, too."

[NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] understood this was not quite what the rule said, but it was what the rule meant. The observatory belonged to him and to Marcos in equal measure, and now Marcos was saying yes, plainly, in one sentence, because this was an answer that could be carried. It meant that when [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] climbed the hill again with Rosa, when they reached the far side and found Elena, he could bring her back across and up the wooden ladder into the space that smelled of stars and dust and the work of their own hands.

The evening was cooling toward its end. The light had taken on the quality it always did near sunset—neither truly gold nor truly orange, but something between that made ordinary things look like they were being remembered rather than seen. [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] and Marcos walked together through the house, through the garden where the olive trees cast their long shadows, to the fig tree with its wooden ladder and the treehouse observatory perched in the branches like a bird's careful nest.

Bruno preceded them, his tail high, no tension in his body now—only the simple certainty of a dog who knew his person was safe and his place was beside him.

Marcos climbed first, his movements slow and deliberate, his walking stick left below. [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] followed, feeling the wooden rungs solid beneath his feet, a ladder built by his grandfather's hands and his own patience. The treehouse creaked the way it always did, and that sound was home now, was proof of making something that lasted.

Inside, the space was smaller than the sky it held. The window Marcos had scavenged fitted perfectly, and through it the emerging stars were beginning to appear like small, patient lights. The cardboard telescope stood in its place. The boards around the walls were still marked with [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO]'s pencil labeling: Polaris, Altair, the shape of Cassiopeia he had traced and retraced until he could see it without looking.

Together, without speaking, they climbed to the high shelf where light fell clearest and longest. Marcos held steady while [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] placed Captain Crunch in the exact center—the fossil shaped like a sleeping animal or a ship's anchor, depending on the light. Around it, in a careful circle, he arranged the smooth stones from the jar, each one chosen for its shape or color or the way light moved through it. Forty-three treasures that the earth had given up and that he and Elena both understood how to see.

The light was extraordinary there—the last of the day catching the pale shell of the fossil and the smooth curves of the stones, turning them gold and then copper and then something that had no name. Looking at them, [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] could almost see the rooms where they had been found: the beach at Cadaques, the riverbed that rushed only in spring, the rocky shore of a place he had only heard described.

Below them, through the open door of the observatory, Bruno had circled three times and settled into the dust, his body warm and his eyes closed. The evening was settling toward its quiet. The first true stars were appearing, not the fading ghosts of them but the real lights that would remain through the whole night long.

Marcos stood beside [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO], not speaking, his hand resting on one of the wooden supports that held the treehouse steady. His walking stick remained on the ground far below, and for the moment he was simply present: an old man and a young boy, looking together at the things they had gathered, and at the sky opening above them like a door into a country they had only begun to know.

"Next time," [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] said quietly, "we will show her this."

Marcos nodded. He did not need to say yes twice. The treehouse held their answer in the light on the stones, in the dust where Bruno slept, in the stars that were coming out one by one, faithful and patient, the way they always did.

The other side of the hill was not a mystery anymore. But the world beyond it still had room for wonders.

It is small enough that [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] knows all the shopkeepers by their faces and most by name. The baker's daughter is his age. People move slowly in the heat.

## People and Groups

- **[NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO]'s Family** — His parents, who want him safe and home by dusk but who understand a boy must learn the shape of the world. They worry about the dark and about the hill in equal measure. They are wrong about how brave he is, but right about how much the dark frightens him.

- **The Grandfather** — A man who built a wooden treehouse observatory and did not laugh when [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] named a fossil after a cereal. He knows more about the hill than he tells. He wants [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] to find his own answers. He walks slowly and tells stories that circle around the truth rather than naming it.

- **The Village** — Shopkeepers, shepherds, the baker and her family: people who have lived here for generations and who have opinions about the hill that range from disinterest to respect. They think the hill is private in a way that has nothing to do with ownership. They are right about that.

- **Whoever Is on the Other Side** — Not yet known. Not yet met. The reason for the journey.

## Rules

- **R1.** [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] must stop travelling when the sun touches the horizon, wherever he is—at home or on either side of the hill. Waiting for daylight where he has stopped is obedience to this rule, not a breach of it.

- **R2.** When Bruno whines and presses his body against [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO]'s leg, that is a warning he must notice, weigh, and speak aloud about, but may choose to go forward past. When Bruno stops dead and turns back, that is a refusal and [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] goes no further that way.

- **R3.** The wooden treehouse observatory belongs to both [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] and his grandfather; neither may promise it or lend it without the other saying yes.

- **R4.** When the sun is fully down, distance becomes unreliable—a path [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] knows in daylight becomes unfindable, and walking further only carries him further from where he meant to be rather than nearer. Fear in the dark is not a small thing.

- **R5.** Supper is at the same hour every night, and the family sits to it then. Whoever is not yet home has a place laid and a plate kept warm until he arrives.

- **R6.** When asked a direct question out of curiosity, the grandfather answers truthfully but in a story that circles the answer. When the same question is asked by someone who has already been to the place and can carry the answer, he answers plainly and in one sentence.

- **R7.** The hill does not shout—voices carry differently there, and distances are harder to judge; a person calling from the other side sounds both nearer and farther than she truly is.

# Chapter 10 — The Other Side Now

The last plate was cleared and his mother had begun to stack them by habit, the rhythm of any ordinary evening, when [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] looked up from the table and asked the question plainly.

"Can I climb the hill again soon? With the same rule—home before dark?"

His father set down his glass and considered this not as a breach but as a reasonable request from a boy who had climbed a hill and lived to ask for another morning. His mother's hand paused on the table. Marcos, still in the corner chair, did not move.

"Yes," his father said. "The same rule holds."

This was exactly the answer [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] had hoped for and somehow did not expect. He felt something settle in his chest—not the hammering anticipation that had driven him up the hill four days ago, but something quieter: the knowledge that the world was larger than he had believed, and that he could move through it again.

Before he could speak further, there was a sound at the gate—a small, polite knock. It was Rosa, flour dust still on her sleeves though the bakery had closed hours ago. She stood in the kitchen doorway with the air of someone who had been waiting and had finally decided on courage.

"[NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO]?" she said, her words tumbling out quickly. "My mother said you would tell me everything about the other side, and I said you would not dare to, and then I said I would come and make you, and I have been at the gate since supper started because I was nervous about interrupting, but now I am here." She stopped for breath. "Can I come next time? When you climb again? I promise I am not afraid of the dark—well, I am, but only a small amount, and I can carry things."

[NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] felt Bruno shift against his leg, tail thumping softly. He looked at Rosa's determined face and understood that she had been waiting not to hear the story, but to be asked into the next one.

"Yes," he said. "Come with us."

His mother smiled in the way that suggested this was exactly what she had meant when she said he would want to tell Rosa everything. Marcos tapped his walking stick once against the floor—not twice, not yet—and his eyes moved between the two children with an expression of quiet approval.

It was only after Rosa had been sent home with a promise to prepare supplies and a piece of his mother's bread that [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] remembered the other thing, the thing he had been turning over in his mind since he woke this morning.

He thought of Elena in her yard on the far side of the hill, bent over the earth looking for what it had left behind. He thought of showing her the wooden treehouse observatory that he and Marcos had built together, the one that smelled of dust and pencil marks and time. He thought of her climbing the wooden ladder nailed into the fig tree and seeing the lens polished by his own hands, the cardboard telescope, the boards he had labeled with stars—and then he remembered the truth of it, the rule that lived inside it.

He looked at Marcos.

"Can I show Elena the observatory?" he asked aloud, the way a question should be asked.

The kitchen was still. His mother's hands were quiet on a bowl. His father was watching. Bruno's ears pricked forward, attentive to the tone of something important being said.

Marcos set down his walking stick and tapped it twice against the stone floor.

Tap. Tap.

The sound of truth about to be spoken.

"Yes," Marcos said, his voice steady and thin as old paper. "It is half hers now, too."

[NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] understood this was not quite what the rule said, but it was what the rule meant. The observatory belonged to him and to Marcos in equal measure, and now Marcos was saying yes, plainly, in one sentence, because this was an answer that could be carried. It meant that when [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] climbed the hill again with Rosa, when they reached the far side and found Elena, he could bring her back across and up the wooden ladder into the space that smelled of stars and dust and the work of their own hands.

The evening was cooling toward its end. The light had taken on the quality it always did near sunset—neither truly gold nor truly orange, but something between that made ordinary things look like they were being remembered rather than seen. [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] and Marcos walked together through the house, through the garden where the olive trees cast their long shadows, to the fig tree with its wooden ladder and the treehouse observatory perched in the branches like a bird's careful nest.

Bruno preceded them, his tail high, no tension in his body now—only the simple certainty of a dog who knew his person was safe and his place was beside him.

Marcos climbed first, his movements slow and deliberate, his walking stick left below. [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] followed, feeling the wooden rungs solid beneath his feet, a ladder built by his grandfather's hands and his own patience. The treehouse creaked the way it always did, and that sound was home now, was proof of making something that lasted.

Inside, the space was smaller than the sky it held. The window Marcos had scavenged fitted perfectly, and through it the emerging stars were beginning to appear like small, patient lights. The cardboard telescope stood in its place. The boards around the walls were still marked with [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO]'s pencil labeling: Polaris, Altair, the shape of Cassiopeia he had traced and retraced until he could see it without looking.

Together, without speaking, they climbed to the high shelf where light fell clearest and longest. Marcos held steady while [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] placed Captain Crunch in the exact center—the fossil shaped like a sleeping animal or a ship's anchor, depending on the light. Around it, in a careful circle, he arranged the smooth stones from the jar, each one chosen for its shape or color or the way light moved through it. Forty-three treasures that the earth had given up and that he and Elena both understood how to see.

The light was extraordinary there—the last of the day catching the pale shell of the fossil and the smooth curves of the stones, turning them gold and then copper and then something that had no name. Looking at them, [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] could almost see the rooms where they had been found: the beach at Cadaques, the riverbed that rushed only in spring, the rocky shore of a place he had only heard described.

Below them, through the open door of the observatory, Bruno had circled three times and settled into the dust, his body warm and his eyes closed. The evening was settling toward its quiet. The first true stars were appearing, not the fading ghosts of them but the real lights that would remain through the whole night long.

Marcos stood beside [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO], not speaking, his hand resting on one of the wooden supports that held the treehouse steady. His walking stick remained on the ground far below, and for the moment he was simply present: an old man and a young boy, looking together at the things they had gathered, and at the sky opening above them like a door into a country they had only begun to know.

"Next time," [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] said quietly, "we will show her this."

Marcos nodded. He did not need to say yes twice. The treehouse held their answer in the light on the stones, in the dust where Bruno slept, in the stars that were coming out one by one, faithful and patient, the way they always did.

The other side of the hill was not a mystery anymore. But the world beyond it still had room for wonders.

# Chapter 10 — The Other Side Now

The last plate was cleared and his mother had begun to stack them by habit, the rhythm of any ordinary evening, when [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] looked up from the table and asked the question plainly.

"Can I climb the hill again soon? With the same rule—home before dark?"

His father set down his glass and considered this not as a breach but as a reasonable request from a boy who had climbed a hill and lived to ask for another morning. His mother's hand paused on the table. Marcos, still in the corner chair, did not move.

"Yes," his father said. "The same rule holds."

This was exactly the answer [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] had hoped for and somehow did not expect. He felt something settle in his chest—not the hammering anticipation that had driven him up the hill four days ago, but something quieter: the knowledge that the world was larger than he had believed, and that he could move through it again.

Before he could speak further, there was a sound at the gate—a small, polite knock. It was Rosa, flour dust still on her sleeves though the bakery had closed hours ago. She stood in the kitchen doorway with the air of someone who had been waiting and had finally decided on courage.

"[NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO]?" she said, her words tumbling out quickly. "My mother said you would tell me everything about the other side, and I said you would not dare to, and then I said I would come and make you, and I have been at the gate since supper started because I was nervous about interrupting, but now I am here." She stopped for breath. "Can I come next time? When you climb again? I promise I am not afraid of the dark—well, I am, but only a small amount, and I can carry things."

[NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] felt Bruno shift against his leg, tail thumping softly. He looked at Rosa's determined face and understood that she had been waiting not to hear the story, but to be asked into the next one.

"Yes," he said. "Come with us."

His mother smiled in the way that suggested this was exactly what she had meant when she said he would want to tell Rosa everything. Marcos tapped his walking stick once against the floor—not twice, not yet—and his eyes moved between the two children with an expression of quiet approval.

It was only after Rosa had been sent home with a promise to prepare supplies and a piece of his mother's bread that [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] remembered the other thing, the thing he had been turning over in his mind since he woke this morning.

He thought of Elena in her yard on the far side of the hill, bent over the earth looking for what it had left behind. He thought of showing her the wooden treehouse observatory that he and Marcos had built together, the one that smelled of dust and pencil marks and time. He thought of her climbing the wooden ladder nailed into the fig tree and seeing the lens polished by his own hands, the cardboard telescope, the boards he had labeled with stars—and then he remembered the truth of it, the rule that lived inside it.

He looked at Marcos.

"Can I show Elena the observatory?" he asked aloud, the way a question should be asked.

The kitchen was still. His mother's hands were quiet on a bowl. His father was watching. Bruno's ears pricked forward, attentive to the tone of something important being said.

Marcos set down his walking stick and tapped it twice against the stone floor.

Tap. Tap.

The sound of truth about to be spoken.

"Yes," Marcos said, his voice steady and thin as old paper. "It is half hers now, too."

[NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] understood this was not quite what the rule said, but it was what the rule meant. The observatory belonged to him and to Marcos in equal measure, and now Marcos was saying yes, plainly, in one sentence, because this was an answer that could be carried. It meant that when [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] climbed the hill again with Rosa, when they reached the far side and found Elena, he could bring her back across and up the wooden ladder into the space that smelled of stars and dust and the work of their own hands.

The evening was cooling toward its end. The light had taken on the quality it always did near sunset—neither truly gold nor truly orange, but something between that made ordinary things look like they were being remembered rather than seen. [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] and Marcos walked together through the house, through the garden where the olive trees cast their long shadows, to the fig tree with its wooden ladder and the treehouse observatory perched in the branches like a bird's careful nest.

Bruno preceded them, his tail high, no tension in his body now—only the simple certainty of a dog who knew his person was safe and his place was beside him.

Marcos climbed first, his movements slow and deliberate, his walking stick left below. [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] followed, feeling the wooden rungs solid beneath his feet, a ladder built by his grandfather's hands and his own patience. The treehouse creaked the way it always did, and that sound was home now, was proof of making something that lasted.

Inside, the space was smaller than the sky it held. The window Marcos had scavenged fitted perfectly, and through it the emerging stars were beginning to appear like small, patient lights. The cardboard telescope stood in its place. The boards around the walls were still marked with [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO]'s pencil labeling: Polaris, Altair, the shape of Cassiopeia he had traced and retraced until he could see it without looking.

Together, without speaking, they climbed to the high shelf where light fell clearest and longest. Marcos held steady while [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] placed Captain Crunch in the exact center—the fossil shaped like a sleeping animal or a ship's anchor, depending on the light. Around it, in a careful circle, he arranged the smooth stones from the jar, each one chosen for its shape or color or the way light moved through it. Forty-three treasures that the earth had given up and that he and Elena both understood how to see.

The light was extraordinary there—the last of the day catching the pale shell of the fossil and the smooth curves of the stones, turning them gold and then copper and then something that had no name. Looking at them, [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] could almost see the rooms where they had been found: the beach at Cadaques, the riverbed that rushed only in spring, the rocky shore of a place he had only heard described.

Below them, through the open door of the observatory, Bruno had circled three times and settled into the dust, his body warm and his eyes closed. The evening was settling toward its quiet. The first true stars were appearing, not the fading ghosts of them but the real lights that would remain through the whole night long.

Marcos stood beside [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO], not speaking, his hand resting on one of the wooden supports that held the treehouse steady. His walking stick remained on the ground far below, and for the moment he was simply present: an old man and a young boy, looking together at the things they had gathered, and at the sky opening above them like a door into a country they had only begun to know.

"Next time," [NOMBRE_ANONIMIZADO] said quietly, "we will show her this."

Marcos nodded. He did not need to say yes twice. The treehouse held their answer in the light on the stones, in the dust where Bruno slept, in the stars that were coming out one by one, faithful and patient, the way they always did.

The other side of the hill was not a mystery anymore. But the world beyond it still had room for wonders.
